stem: In a **site-and-service scheme**, what does the council provide?

options.content: Plots with roads, water and sewers
options.rationale: Correct: families then build their own houses.

options.content: Fully built houses at no cost
options.rationale: Houses are built by the families themselves.

options.content: Free bus travel to the CBD
options.rationale: That is a transport policy.

options.content: Farmland for growing crops
options.rationale: Site-and-service is a housing scheme.

explanation: The council provides serviced plots; residents build homes.

stem: What is the main purpose of a **green belt**?

options.content: To restrict urban sprawl into the countryside
options.rationale: Correct: building is restricted in the protected zone.

options.content: To grow trees for firewood in the CBD
options.rationale: Green belts surround the city, not the CBD.

options.content: To provide land for new factories
options.rationale: Green belts restrict building.

options.content: To store floodwater in the city centre after storms
options.rationale: That is the role of parks or detention ponds.

explanation: Green belts protect open land around cities.

stem: Which strategy most directly reduces traffic congestion in a city centre?

options.content: A frequent bus rapid transit system
options.rationale: Correct: buses carry many more people per vehicle than cars.

options.content: A site-and-service housing scheme
options.rationale: This addresses housing, not traffic.

options.content: A new landfill site
options.rationale: This addresses waste.

options.content: Upgrading an informal settlement
options.rationale: This addresses housing conditions.

explanation: Efficient public transport takes cars off the road.

stem: Why did Zimbabwe develop **growth points** such as Gokwe and Murambinda?

options.content: To build new high-density suburbs on the edge of Harare
options.rationale: Growth points are rural centres, not suburbs.

options.content: To replace the central business district of Bulawayo
options.rationale: They were not designed to replace city centres.

options.content: To create green belts round Harare
options.rationale: Green belts are protected open land.

options.content: To bring jobs and services to rural areas
options.rationale: Correct: growth points tackle push factors.

explanation: Growth points decentralise development to rural areas.

stem: Which town was developed south of Harare largely to house people who work in Harare?

options.content: Kariba
options.rationale: Kariba is a resort and HEP town on the Zambezi.

options.content: Chitungwiza
options.rationale: Correct: it is a satellite (largely dormitory) town of Harare.

options.content: Hwange
options.rationale: Hwange is a coal-mining town in the north-west.

options.content: Beitbridge
options.rationale: Beitbridge is a border town on the Limpopo.

explanation: Chitungwiza grew as a satellite town for Harare workers.

stem: Which feature of Curitiba, Brazil, is an example of sustainable urban transport?

options.content: New motorways through the city centre
options.rationale: Motorways encourage more car use.

options.content: Free parking for all cars in the CBD
options.rationale: Free parking encourages car use.

options.content: Bus rapid transit with dedicated lanes
options.rationale: Correct: fast, high-capacity buses reduce car use.

options.content: Banning all public buses
options.rationale: This would increase car use.

explanation: Curitiba's BRT is a well-known sustainable transport scheme.

stem: A satellite town was built 25 km from a capital city, but almost all its residents still work in the capital. What problem is most likely?

options.content: A shortage of workers in the satellite town's factories
options.rationale: Few factories exist there, so this is unlikely.

options.content: Long, costly commuting and congestion on the main road
options.rationale: Correct: it has become a dormitory town.

options.content: Rapid loss of population from the satellite town
options.rationale: People still live there; the issue is commuting.

options.content: Falling land values in the capital's CBD
options.rationale: Commuting into the CBD keeps demand high.

explanation: Without local jobs, satellite towns generate commuter traffic.
hints: Where do the residents of the new town work?

stem: Which is the main weakness of site-and-service schemes for the poorest urban families?

options.content: The plots have no water or sewer connections
options.rationale: Providing these services is the point of the scheme.

options.content: Families are not allowed to build their own houses
options.rationale: Self-building is part of the scheme.

options.content: The schemes are always located in the central business district
options.rationale: They are usually on the edge of the town.

options.content: They may still be unable to afford the plot and building materials
options.rationale: Correct: costs can exclude the poorest.

hints: Consider who can afford each option.

stem: Recycling can reduce the amount of waste sent to landfill and create jobs.
explanation: True. Recycling reduces landfill and supports collectors and processors.

stem: Building more roads always reduces traffic congestion permanently.
explanation: False. New roads often attract more traffic; public transport and planning are also needed.

stem: Match each urban problem with a suitable management strategy.

payload.template: A satellite town whose residents mostly work in the main city is called a {{blank:a}} town. A city that uses sensors and data to manage traffic and energy is a {{blank:b}} city.

explanation: Dormitory towns house commuters; smart cities use digital technology.

stem: A bus carries 120 passengers. Cars in a fictional city carry an average of 1.5 people (fictional data). How many cars would be needed to carry the same number of people as one full bus?
A fictional site-and-service scheme of 2,500 plots costs US\$ 3,000,000 for roads and US\$ 4,500,000 for water and sewer pipes (fictional data). Calculate the cost per plot in US dollars.
hints: Divide by the number of plots.

stem: Suggest **four** solutions to the problems caused by rapid urbanisation, linking each to a problem.

points.description: Housing shortage: site-and-service or low-cost housing schemes.
Congestion: better public transport (buses, commuter trains) / ring roads.
Water and sanitation: repair and expand treatment works and sewers / boreholes.
Waste: regular collection and recycling / migration: growth points and rural development.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Site-and-service schemes ease the housing shortage. More buses and commuter trains reduce congestion. Expanding water treatment works and repairing sewers reduce disease. Regular refuse collection and recycling keep streets clean.

explanation: Each solution must match a problem.

stem: Evaluate satellite towns as a way of managing the growth of a large city.

points.description: Advantage: relieve housing pressure and overcrowding in the main city.
Advantage: can attract industry and services, spreading jobs.
Limitation: often become dormitory towns, causing long commutes and congestion.
Judgement: successful only if jobs and services are provided locally (e.g. Chitungwiza).

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Satellite towns house many people and relieve overcrowding in the main city, and they can attract factories and shops. But if jobs stay in the city, like many in Chitungwiza, residents face long, expensive commutes and the main roads become congested. They work best when local jobs and services are provided.

hints: Give advantages and limitations, then judge.

stem: For a named urban area, describe the challenges caused by its growth and evaluate the strategies used to manage it.

points.description: Names the urban area (e.g. Harare) and the causes of growth.
Challenges: housing shortage, unplanned settlements (e.g. Epworth, Caledonia).
Challenges: water supply and pollution of Lake Chivero, cholera, waste, congestion, unemployment.
Strategy: site-and-service and upgrading; benefits and limits.
Strategy: satellite towns (Chitungwiza, Norton, Ruwa) and growth points; benefits and limits.
Strategy: transport regulation and buses / water and sewer rehabilitation / recycling; benefits and limits.
Overall judgement on success with reasons (funding, scale, maintenance, participation).

levels.descriptor: Developed, accurate explanation of several relevant points, supported by a located example or the resource, with a clear judgement or conclusion where the question asks for one.
Some explanation of relevant points, partly developed; an example or resource evidence is used in general terms; any judgement is simple or one-sided.
Simple statements or a list of points with little explanation; no example or only a name.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Harare has grown rapidly since 1980 through rural-urban migration and natural increase. Housing is short, so many people rent rooms or live in backyard shacks and unplanned settlements such as parts of Epworth and Caledonia. Water treatment and sewers are overloaded, Lake Chivero is polluted, and cholera outbreaks in 2008-09 and 2018 followed. Refuse collection is irregular and roads are congested. Site-and-service schemes have provided many serviced plots, but not enough to clear the waiting list and some are unaffordable for the poorest. Upgrading in Epworth gives residents security and services without moving them, but it is slow and depends on funding. Satellite towns such as Chitungwiza have housed large numbers but created long commutes. Rehabilitation of water works and boreholes has helped some suburbs, but supply still falls short. Overall the strategies have reduced some problems but have not kept pace with growth, mainly because of limited funding and maintenance.

explanation: Case study detail, evaluation of several strategies and a judgement.
hints: Causes, challenges, opportunities, management, then evaluation.
Use real place names in your city.

stem:
A fictional city council has US\$ 20 million to spend. It is considering three projects (fictional data).

| Project | Cost (US\$ million) | Main benefit | People helped |
|---|---|---|---|
| P: bus rapid transit corridor | 18 | Faster, cheaper commuting | 90,000 daily passengers |
| Q: site-and-service plots | 12 | 4,000 serviced plots | about 20,000 residents |
| R: sewer repairs in old high-density suburbs | 8 | Fewer sewage overflows | about 150,000 residents |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Which combination of projects can the council afford within its budget?

options.content: P and Q
options.rationale: 18 + 12 = US\$ 30 million is over budget.

options.content: P and R
options.rationale: 18 + 8 = US\$ 26 million is over budget.

options.content: Q and R
options.rationale: Correct: 12 + 8 = US\$ 20 million.

options.content: P, Q and R
options.rationale: 38 million is far over budget.

parts.explanation: Only Q and R together fit the US\$ 20 million budget.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the cost per plot of Project Q in US dollars.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Recommend which project(s) the council should choose. Justify your answer.

points.description: Clear recommendation (e.g. Q and R together, as they fit the budget).
R helps the most people (150,000) at the lowest cost, reducing disease.
Q provides housing for about 20,000 people, easing the shortage.
Recognises the trade-off: P would help commuters but uses most of the budget alone.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The council should choose Q and R, which together cost exactly US\$ 20 million. Sewer repairs help about 150,000 people for only US\$ 8 million and reduce cholera risk, while the plots house about 20,000 people. The bus corridor would help commuters but would use almost the whole budget.

parts.explanation: Justify with data and acknowledge what is lost.

explanation: This item practises evaluating urban management options with data.
hints: Check which combinations fit the budget.

stem:
Table 1 shows average journey times into a fictional city centre before and after a bus rapid transit (BRT) line opened (fictional data).

| Mode | Before BRT (minutes) | After BRT (minutes) |
|---|---|---|
| Car | 55 | 48 |
| Ordinary bus | 70 | 66 |
| BRT bus | — | 35 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: How many minutes faster is the BRT bus than a car after the BRT opened?

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the percentage fall in car journey time. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Suggest why car journeys also became faster after the BRT opened.

points.description: Some drivers switched to the BRT, so fewer cars were on the road.
Less congestion at junctions and in the CBD.
Dedicated bus lanes removed buses from the general traffic lanes / fewer buses stopping in traffic.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Some commuters left their cars and used the faster BRT, so there were fewer cars on the roads. The buses also ran in their own lanes, so they no longer blocked other traffic at stops.

parts.explanation: Link modal shift to reduced congestion.

explanation: This item practises evaluating a transport strategy with data.
hints: Subtract to find the time saved.
